means: Witches keep raising Skeletons, which distract defences and soak up shots. In our plan, Golems lead and Witches follow through a gap made by Wall Breakers or a Jump Spell. It does not take precise timing.
Guides differ on the details. Some put Witches on two corners first, with Healers, to make a funnel, and then send a Golem and heroes into the core. Army names like this are often used loosely.
glossary.example: Golems first to take the fire, then Witches behind them, then Rage, Freeze and Healing as needed.

glossary.short: The Archer Queen and a group of Healers moving around the base together.
means: Healers follow the Archer Queen and heal the damage she takes. With four or five of them she can go on removing buildings for a long time.
Her usual job is clearing the edge of a base to set up a funnel, or removing one chosen target. Air Defenses are the danger, because when they kill the Healers she falls quickly.
glossary.example: Walk the Queen down one side with her Healers, keeping clear of Air Defenses, then send the main army.

glossary.short: The Archer Queen with Healers, sent to clear a whole side before the army follows.
means: It uses the same pair as a Queen Walk, but gives her a bigger job. With four to six Healers and spells, she removes several key defences and clears one side, often after Wall Breakers have got her into a compartment.

Our Queen Charge plans follow with a Hybrid of Hog Riders and Miners. Other follow-ups are possible, such as LaLoon. Some guides, and at times ours, use Queen Walk and Queen Charge for the same thing. QC is the short form.
glossary.example: Walk the Queen with Healers on one side, keeping her away from single target Inferno Towers, then send Hog Riders and Miners.

glossary.short: RC means Royal Champion. Here she clears a route while spells keep her alive.
means: RC is short for Royal Champion. She has short range and goes for defences, jumping walls to do so. In an RC Walk you keep her alive with Invisibility Spells, so she takes out defence after defence and leaves a funnel behind her.

When the walk is finished, your Dragons or Root Riders follow along the side she cleared. Blueprint suggests recalling her once the Invisibility runs out. It takes precise control, because a badly placed spell loses her.
glossary.example: Walk the Royal Champion with Invisibility, then send Root Riders with Overgrowth along the cleared side.

glossary.short: The Royal Champion sent in to strip key defences as part of the main attack.
means: In an RC Charge she goes after particular defences, such as a Spell Tower or those around the Town Hall. Electro Boots and Invisibility are common choices for keeping her alive.

Our plans differ on timing. Some charge her along one side first, and others send her behind a tank and Super Yetis. Guides overlap with RC Walk too, so treat the name as a rough guide and read the steps.
glossary.example: Charge the Royal Champion along one side, then send Root Riders through the defences she has weakened.

glossary.short: The Dragon Duke sent into the base first, with an air army following.
means: The Dragon Duke is a tough flying hero who gets stronger when no friendly flyers are near him. A Duke Charge uses that. He goes in alone, supported by spells such as Invisibility, Revive or Totem, and clears what he can before the rest fly in.

Keep your other air troops away from him at first, or they switch off the bonus. Our plan follows with Inferno Dragons, a Lava Hound, Rocket Balloons and Dragon Riders. Blueprint's version has Dragons sweeping up behind him.
glossary.example: Charge the Dragon Duke along one side using Invisibility, then send your air troops on a different lane.

glossary.short: The Grand Warden and Healers moving round the base to clear a side.
means: The Grand Warden has long range and little health, so Healers keep him going while he shoots. Blueprint uses him with Healers and Furnaces to make the funnel, before the main group arrives.
It works like a Queen Walk, though you also have his ability and his Fireball, if he wears it, to think about. Keep the ability back for the moment it is most needed.
glossary.example: Open with the Warden and Healers on one side, then fire his Fireball at a stack of defences.

glossary.short: The Grand Warden leads with Healers, and the main army pushes in behind him.
means: Our Warden Charge Super Yetis plan opens with the Warden and Healers, uses Furnaces and Skeleton Spells to pull fire, and then sends Super Yetis behind him, with Jump where walls block them.
It is loosely named. Blueprint calls the opening of this same army a Warden walk, so the two names can mean the same thing.
glossary.example: Warden and Healers first, then Super Yetis behind, with a Jump Spell on the blocking wall.

glossary.short: A heavy ground attack led by Root Riders, which break walls very quickly.
means: Root Riders are tough ground troops that smash walls and go for defences, so walls hold them up far less than most ground troops. A group of them goes through a walled base with Overgrowth and Rage helping. Trophy Coach calls Root Rider smash the most consistent high Town Hall ground army of 2026.

Our Root Rider Yeti is one form of it. Root Riders push the defences and Super Yetis follow into the core, with a hero charge alongside. Its weak point is the Monolith, which hits high health troops hardest.
glossary.example: The King and Giants make the funnel, then Root Riders go in, followed by Super Yetis into the core.

glossary.short: Yetis sent behind a tank to overwhelm the base on the ground.
means: Yetis hit hard, and they release small Yetimites as they take damage, which add to the pressure. Sent through a funnel behind a tank such as an Ice Golem, they flood the core.
It is a ground alternative to Dragons from about TH12. Multi-target Inferno Towers are its main problem, as they cut through a swarm.
glossary.example: Make a funnel with heroes, send Yetis behind an Ice Golem, then Rage and Freeze as they reach the core.

glossary.short: Dragons followed by a swarm from Bat Spells.
means: The name joins Dragons and Bats. Dragons go first and deal with what would kill Bats quickly, such as Wizard Towers and other splash defences. Bat Spells then flood the part of the base that is left.

Bats die quickly to splash, so timing decides the attack. AllClash's older guide has a slightly different split, with Dragons on the side away from the Air Defenses and Bats taking those Air Defenses.
glossary.example: Deploy Dragons with a Battle Blimp, wait until the splash defences are gone, then drop Bat Spells outside the rest.

glossary.short: Short for suicide. Heroes dive early to remove defences, without being expected to survive.
means: In a sui, heroes and a few tanks go deep early on to remove key defences. They may well not come back, and that is fine if they took out enough. Players talk about the value of a sui, meaning what it removed.
It is usually the first half of an attack. The classic form is Sui Lalo, where Lava Hounds and Balloons follow through the space it opened.
glossary.example: Sui Lalo at TH12: a Golem and Ice Golem tank for the heroes, then Lava Hounds and Balloons finish the base.

glossary.short: Grand Warden equipment that throws an explosion at the closest defence. Armies are named after it.
means: Fireball is epic hero equipment for the Grand Warden. When fired, it throws a big exploding ball at the closest defence, which can flatten a group of defences that sit close together. Fireball Super Yeti opens the base this way and then sends Super Yetis through the hole.

Trophy Coach warns that it needs a high level to work well, at about level 24. Below that, it may leave a damaged defence standing and not the empty space you planned for. Aim is set by where the Warden stands, so walk him to the right spot first.
glossary.example: Soften defences with the Warden's Fireball, then send Super Yetis with the King and Royal Champion.

glossary.short: Dragon Duke equipment that flies him in a straight line across the base.
means: When fired, the Dragon Duke flies across the base in a straight line, breathing fire. While flying he cannot be targeted, traps do not go off, and the Clan Castle stays inactive.

Line up the angle first, since a poor line wastes most of its value. He lands exposed on the far side, so have follow-up ready, or a Recall Spell. Rocket Backpack Throwers opens with this flight, then sends Throwers and Healers.
glossary.example: Open with the Dragon Duke on Rocket Backpack, then open walls with Wall Breakers and send Throwers and Healers.

glossary.short: A building that holds troops donated by your clan. Also called the CC.
means: Your clan mates can send you troops, spells and Siege Machines, which sit in your Clan Castle. When you attack, you can drop those troops like any others. A Siege Machine can carry them into the base for you.

On defence, the enemy's castle does the same in reverse. Its troops come out when an attacker gets close, and can stop a hero or a push by surprise. So guides often say to lure them out first, or to plan your path around the castle.
glossary.example: Clan Castle troops can be sent in a Battle Blimp to land next to a key defence.

glossary.short: The main building of a base. TH followed by a number gives its level, as in TH13.
means: Your Town Hall level decides what you can build and which troops, spells and heroes are open to you. Advice is often given by level because the same army can be strong at TH9 and useless at TH14.
It also matters in an attack. Destroying the enemy's Town Hall earns a star on its own.
glossary.example: Root Riders open at TH15, so a Root Rider plan is no use to a TH14 player.

glossary.short: How much room a troop or spell takes up in your army.
means: Your army has a limited amount of room, and each troop takes a set share of it. A Barbarian takes 1, a Dragon 20, a Golem 30. A strong troop costs more than a weak one, so every army is a trade-off.

Spells use their own separate space, and the same word applies. A Haste Spell takes one space and a Revive Spell two. Some effects also depend on it, such as the Eagle Artillery, which waits until 200 housing has been deployed.
glossary.example: A Yeti takes 18 housing and a Super Yeti takes 35, so boosting it changes how many you can bring.

glossary.short: Damage that hits everything in an area, not just one target.
means: Splash hits the target and whatever stands near it. Mortars, Wizard Towers and Bomb Towers use it against your troops, so a tight clump of weak troops can vanish in one shot. That is why guides say to spread them out.
It works for you too. Wizards, Baby Dragons and Super Bowlers hit several buildings at once, which suits a packed core. A defence's splash radius tells you how far it reaches.
glossary.example: One Mortar shell can kill a clump of Archers, so drop them in a line.

glossary.short: Hits only one thing at a time.
means: A single target defence or troop puts all its damage on one target and moves on only when that target is gone. It is deadly against a hero or tank, but slow against many small units.

So you beat single target defences with numbers or distractions. Skeletons and swarms waste their shots. Inferno Towers are the main example, because a single target Inferno builds up the longer it stays on one target.
glossary.example: Keep your Queen clear of single target Inferno Towers, or Freeze them as they lock on.

glossary.short: Hits several separate targets at the same moment.
means: A multi-target defence fires at several enemies at once, with less damage on each than a single target one. It is at its best against swarms of small troops and weak against one big tank.
An Inferno Tower can be set by its owner to single or multi-target, so check which it is when you scout. A Multi-Archer Tower hits three targets at once.
glossary.example: Multi-target Inferno Towers cut through a swarm of Yetis and Yetimites.

glossary.short: An attack that jumps from one target to others close by.
means: A chain attack hits one target and then leaps to the next one in reach, usually for less damage each time. Spacing decides how well it does. Close buildings or close troops take more hits, and spread ones break the chain.

It works in both directions. Electro Dragons and Super Wizards chain through your enemy's buildings. A Super Wizard Tower chains through your troops, up to 15 targets, and a Ricochet Cannon's shot bounces on to a second target.
glossary.example: Send Electro Dragons in a straight line through buildings that sit close together.

glossary.short: An area around a unit that affects everything nearby.
means: An aura goes with the unit and affects things inside its range. Some help your troops, as with the Apprentice Warden, whose aura gives nearby troops extra health. Others hurt the enemy, as with the Electro Titan, whose aura damages everything around her.
To get the most from a helping aura, drop it where the most friends will stand inside it, usually mid-group and not at the front.
glossary.example: Walk an Apprentice Warden with tough troops, since his aura only reaches 7 tiles.

glossary.short: Melee means hitting at arm's length. Ranged means shooting from further off.
means: A melee unit has to walk right up to its target, so walls and other troops can hold it up, and it takes the fire when it gets there. A ranged unit shoots from a distance, often over walls, and usually has less health.
Reach is why some pets and heroes fit badly together. A pet with short range may run far ahead of a hero who attacks from long range.
glossary.example: Valkyries are melee and need a way through walls, while Archers can shoot over them.

glossary.short: One square of the grid a base is built on, used to measure distance.
means: A base sits on a grid. Each square is a tile. Building sizes such as 3x3 count tiles, and so do ranges and spell sizes.
It helps you place things. Knowing a Healing Spell reaches 5 tiles or a defence shoots 9 tiles tells you where to drop things and who is safe.
glossary.example: Place a Healing Spell 3 to 4 tiles ahead of the group, so they walk into it.

glossary.short: A distance too close for a defence to hit. Also called a blind spot.
means: Some defences cannot shoot anything right next to them. Troops that get inside that distance are safe from that defence and can hit it freely.

The Eagle Artillery cannot hit closer than 7 tiles and the Scattershot closer than 3. The Mortar has a small gap as well. It explains why these defences are hard to deal with from far off, yet simple once your troops are next to them.
glossary.example: Once your troops reach an Eagle Artillery they no longer take its shots, though other defences still hit them.

glossary.short: Small units made by another troop, spell or pet during an attack.
means: You do not train these. They appear during the attack. Skeletons from a Witch are the simplest example. Yetimites come out of Yetis and Super Yetis as they take damage. Golemites and Lava Pups appear when a Golem or Lava Hound falls. Ice Pups do the same for an Ice Hound. Meteormites are the halves a Meteor Golem splits into.

Firemites come from a Furnace. A Super Witch summons a single Big Boy. A Ruin Witch turns rubble, which destroyed buildings leave behind, into Ruin Knights. Frostmites and Boogers come from the pets Frosty and Sneezy.
They can be a real part of your damage, and they keep drawing fire after their parent has gone. Some spells treat them differently. Ice Block, for one, does not cover spawned troops.
glossary.example: Golemites keep drawing fire after a Golem falls, which gives your main troops extra time.

glossary.short: A built-in power-up some troops get when they are alone or angry. Not the Rage Spell.
means: Baby Dragons and the Dragon Duke become enraged when no other friendly flyers are near. They gain extra damage and attack speed while it lasts.
So these units want space. Sending other flyers alongside them, or giving the Duke a pet like Sneezy whose Boogers fly near him, can turn the bonus off.
glossary.example: Use one or two Baby Dragons away from your air group, so each one stays enraged while clearing the outside.

glossary.short: The best result an attack can get: all three stars.
means: An attack can earn three stars. You get one for destroying 50% of the base, one for destroying the Town Hall, and one for destroying everything. A three-star therefore means the whole base went down.
To three-star a base, or an army's three-star rate, is the usual way players judge how good an attack is. A hit rate is the same idea: the share of attacks with an army that got all three.
glossary.example: Mass Dragons is often called the safest three-star at TH7.

glossary.short: A clan against clan contest, decided by total stars.
means: Two clans are matched and face off. After a preparation day comes a battle day, when each member can usually attack twice, and the clan with more stars wins.

Unlike a normal attack, you can study the target base for as long as you like before you start, and you only get limited attempts. So guides favour armies that are reliable, and much advice here is aimed at war.
glossary.example: Greedy Raven is a farming pet, so swap it out before war unless your plan needs its storage damage.

glossary.short: Clan War League: a monthly event where clans play a series of wars.
means: Clan War League runs for part of each month. Your clan plays several wars in a row against other clans in its group, and each member gets one attack per war. Results earn League Medals to spend in a special shop.
With one attack per war, there is no second try, so players look for safe armies. If a guide calls something good for CWL, it usually means dependable.
glossary.example: Base Drop rates the Minion Prince for CWL clean-up rather than as a main carry.

glossary.short: A stronger version of a normal troop that you pay to unlock for a few days.
means: From about TH11, you can boost a troop you have levelled high enough into its super version. A boost costs Dark Elixir, 25,000 in our data, and lasts three days. Super Yeti, Super Archer and Rocket Balloon are examples.
Most take more housing than the normal troop, and most have a special ability of their own. As a boost is costly and time limited, check your plan before you pay.
glossary.example: Boosting Yetis into Super Yetis takes each one from 18 housing to 35.

glossary.short: A vehicle that carries your Clan Castle troops into the base. Built in the Workshop.
means: You build these in the Workshop from TH12 on. Most go somewhere useful, such as to the Town Hall, and release your Clan Castle troops when they finish or are destroyed. Some do the job in a different way, like a Log Launcher that clears walls ahead of it.
Spells mostly do not help them. A Healer will not heal one, and many lose health over time. Clan mates can also donate them to your Clan Castle.
glossary.example: A Wall Wrecker drives at the Town Hall, smashing walls on the way, then releases your Clan Castle troops.

glossary.short: A power you fire by tapping a hero's icon during an attack.
means: Heroes can do things beyond their normal attack. You tap the hero's icon once, and what happens depends on the equipment they wear, such as a burst of healing, a big strike or a shield for the army. You usually get one use in an attack.

Timing is often the difference between a hero surviving or not. Fire it too early and it is gone when the big hit comes. Fire it too late and the hero has already fallen. Some troops have named abilities of their own, which work without you doing anything.
glossary.example: Save the Warden's ability until the push is under heavy fire, not the moment you can use it.

glossary.short: Items a hero wears that change what they can do, upgraded with ore at the Blacksmith.
means: Each hero wears two pieces at a time, chosen from a set made for that hero. The Blacksmith opens at TH8 and upgrades them using ore. Shiny Ore is the most common, Glowy Ore is rarer, and Starry Ore is the rarest and only goes on epic pieces.

Common pieces come free as you upgrade the Blacksmith and reach level 18. Epic pieces come from events, the season shop or the Trader and reach level 27. Rarity does not always mean stronger, so check what your plan needs.
glossary.example: Spiky Ball is the usual first pick for the King. Earthquake Boots suit pushes that need walls broken.

glossary.short: Grand Warden equipment that makes him and nearby troops immune to damage for a moment.
means: When fired, the Grand Warden and friendly units close to him take no damage for a short time. It is the safest first upgrade for him, since it helps in almost any army.

Use it for the worst moment of the attack, such as when a group walks into a nest of defences. Fire it the moment it is ready and you have nothing left for that. It is a piece of equipment, so a Warden not wearing it does not have it. An Apprentice Warden never does.
glossary.example: Save the Tome until your Yetis reach the core, then fire it as the Inferno Towers and bombs start hitting.

glossary.short: The two ways a Grand Warden can move, on foot or flying.
means: You choose before you deploy him. In ground mode he walks with ground troops and can walk over walls. In air mode he flies with an air army, and air-hitting defences can target him instead of ground ones.
Choose by the army he has to stay with, since his support only reaches nearby troops. Some pets suit one mode better. Boogers from Sneezy, for example, are said to work in air mode only.
An X-Bow has modes too, though for a different reason. Its owner sets it to ground only at long range, or to air and ground at a shorter 11.5 tiles.
glossary.example: Walk him on foot with Super Yetis, and fly him with Dragons.

glossary.short: Extra upgrade stages for a building already at its final level.
means: When a building is fully upgraded at the top Town Hall, you can spend a builder and resources on small extra boosts. A defence usually gets two stages, each adding a bit of damage or health. They are cheaper and smaller than a normal upgrade.

They do not last forever. When Supercell releases a new level for that building, its supercharges reset. For an attacker, it means a top level defence can be a little stronger than its level suggests.

glossary.short: Two defences at high levels combined into one stronger building.
means: From TH16, you can merge two maxed defences to make a new one. Two Archer Towers at level 21 become a Multi-Archer Tower, and two Cannons at level 21 become a Ricochet Cannon.

A Multi-Gear Tower at TH17 takes a geared up Archer Tower and a geared up Cannon. At TH18, two level 17 Wizard Towers become a Super Wizard Tower. Each has an attack the originals lacked, so old advice about those buildings no longer fits.
glossary.example: A Ricochet Cannon's shot bounces on to a second target, so a line of troops is not as safe as it once was.

glossary.short: A Builder Base upgrade that gives a home defence a second way of firing.
means: A Cannon, an Archer Tower and a Mortar can each be geared up once you have their partner building on the Builder Base. The Master Builder does the work, and it costs home village Gold. You need the defence at the listed level too.

A geared up defence gets a new mode. A Cannon or Mortar gets Burst mode, and an Archer Tower gets Fast attack mode. It shoots much faster, though Cannons and Archer Towers lose some range for it. A geared up pair can also feed the Multi-Gear Tower later on.
glossary.example: A geared up Cannon in Burst mode reaches 7 tiles instead of 9 but hits every 0.192 seconds.

glossary.short: A defending unit that protects the Town Hall at TH18. Attackers cannot use them.
means: At TH18, the Town Hall lost its own weapon and gained a Guardian. You pick one to defend at a time: the Smasher, the Longshot or the Logger. It stands on the Town Hall, then jumps down and fights once enemies come within range.

The Smasher is melee, and it hits with splash. It leaves Rage behind when it falls. The Longshot is ranged with splash and explodes when defeated. The Logger rolls slow logs that hit everything in their path and knock targets back.
All of them hit both ground and air, so plan for one as you reach the Town Hall. Clash Ninja's April 2026 notes say Poison works on them at reduced damage, and that they do not wake while Frozen.
glossary.example: Do not walk fragile troops into the Town Hall area without checking which Guardian is on it.

glossary.short: The spells a Spell Tower can cast on the defending side.
means: A Spell Tower casts spells to help the defence, the same way you would on attack. Its options grow by level: Rage from level 1, Poison from level 2, Invisibility from level 3, and Earthquake from level 4.

Rage makes defences hit harder. Poison hurts and slows your troops. Invisibility hides defences for a moment. Earthquake does a share of damage to troops. After casting, it needs 50 to 70 seconds to recharge, so it can fire again in a long attack. Taking one out early, or freezing it when it is about to cast, can save an attack.
glossary.example: Rage from a Spell Tower gives defences 60% extra damage for 18 seconds, so a Freeze on the tower is often well spent.

glossary.short: Short for Inferno Tower, a defence that burns one target or several.
means: In single target mode, the beam grows stronger the longer it stays on the same target, until it melts heroes and tanks. In multi-target mode, it hits several at once for steady damage.
Freeze, Invisibility and Ice Block are the usual answers. Breaking its lock with Invisibility resets the beam, so it has to build up again.
glossary.example: Cast Invisibility on a hero as an Inferno starts to burn, and the beam has to start over.

glossary.short: Short for Hog Riders.
means: Hog Riders jump walls and go straight for defences, so they are fast but easily wiped by traps and splash. Players nearly always call them Hogs.
A Super Hog Rider is a separate boosted troop, so check which one a plan means.
glossary.example: Heal the Hogs where defences overlap.

glossary.short: The Gold, Elixir and Dark Elixir you take from a base you attack.
means: Attacking lets you steal part of what another player holds in their storages and collectors. Destroying those buildings gets you the loot inside.

Loot pays for your upgrades, so it is what players attack for when they are not fighting for stars. A troop or pet that is good for loot goes for those resource buildings, and may not help you win a war.
glossary.example: Goblins run for storages first, so they suit raids for loot but not war.

glossary.short: Attacking mainly to collect resources rather than to win stars.
means: Upgrades are costly, so players spend a lot of attacks raiding for Gold and Elixir. A farming army is cheap and quick to rebuild, and it does not need three stars.

Players look for dead bases, meaning inactive villages whose collectors have filled up. They are full of easy loot, since nobody has been around to collect it. A raid in our guide means this kind of attack.
glossary.example: A Greedy Raven does extra damage to resource buildings, which is why it is a farming pet.

glossary.short: To study a base before you attack it.
means: Before you attack, you look over the base. Note where Air Defenses and Inferno Towers sit, whether each Inferno is single or multi-target, and where traps might be hiding in gaps.
In war you get as long as you like, and Trophy Coach suggests at least 30 seconds. A plan that does not fit the base often fails however well you carry it out.
glossary.example: Check where the Clan Castle reaches, so you know whether your hero will wake its troops.

glossary.short: A free practice attack on a clan mate's base.
means: You can post a challenge in clan chat, and a clan mate can attack your base. Nothing is lost: you keep your troops and spells, and no trophies or loot change hands.
It is the safest place to try an army or a new unit before risking a war attack. Guides are thin on some newer units, so testing here may tell you more.
glossary.example: Try a new army in a friendly challenge before using it in war.

glossary.short: A change by Supercell that makes something stronger.
means: Supercell adjusts troops and defences through balance updates. When something gets stronger, it has been buffed. A buff can make old advice about it out of date.
So a guide written before a buff can undersell what it describes.
glossary.example: Hog Riders had a health buff in October, so older low ratings may no longer be fair.

glossary.short: A change by Supercell that makes something weaker.
means: The opposite of a buff. When a unit is too strong, Supercell cuts its health, damage or something else, and players say it was nerfed.
Figures gathered before a nerf can flatter what they describe, as our guide warns in a few places.
glossary.example: Fire Heart was nerfed in October, so older figures for Dragon Duke armies may overstate them.

glossary.short: Whichever armies and tactics are most popular and effective right now.
means: The meta is what most strong players are using at the moment. It shifts as Supercell changes the game and players find new ideas.
It is a helpful starting point, not a rule. An army can be strong and out of the meta, particularly at lower Town Halls, where the top players' choices matter less.
